deep.reconstruction:
Setting (cote 154, 1983-84): Sigma is a finite system of pseudo-lines in the real projective plane X, with X~ its double cover (the 2-sphere). Grothendieck studies the set of 'positions' of an extra pseudo-line D relative to Sigma. A position is stable (generic) if D passes through no vertex of Sigma, and non-stable if it passes through vertices. These positions are organised into a graph or poset Gamma(Sigma) by 'specialisation' (moving D onto a vertex) and its inverse, which he writes 'généralisation/générisation'. The previous page introduced 'triangles de spécialisation' and 'cuvettes': a stable D specialises by sweeping across a triangular cell or sector of the arrangement whose base lies on D.

This page has two parts.

(1) Left column. When there is such a triangle, the orientation of D is fixed by its being the base of specialisation triangles; the figure has two of them. The difficulty is that the specialisations, with their orientations, do not combine with the other immediate specialisations and generalisations into a natural polygonal structure when there are several. So he changes viewpoint: start from a non-stable position Delta and study its immediate generalisations. The coloured figure shows Delta (orange) through two star-shaped multiple points. Perturbed strands (green, blue, yellow) are pushed off the vertices to one side or the other, with small arrows marking the push. He notes two generalisations per edge ('A. bleus') and orientation, along the orientation of Delta.

(2) Right column. At each vertex of Sigma on Delta there are likewise two local generalisations, one for each side of X at that vertex. Delta lifts to a closed curve in X~, a topological polygon whose vertices and edges come from Sigma. He warns that this polygon is not canonical as such: it depends on a choice, essentially an orientation of Delta. His claim is that the immediate generalisations of Delta are identified with the vertices of a polygon of order 2nu. A general, non-immediate count gives 2nu + 2nu = 4nu, corrected in the footnote to 2nu for immediate ones. This polygon is a double covering (order 2) of the polygon defined by Delta, and an orientation of it corresponds to an orientation of Delta.

Aim: to show that each non-stable position has a link that is a circle (a polygon). This is the local condition for the complex of positions, Gamma(Sigma) with its 2-cells, to be a topological surface. The next page carries this out for the lifted D~, treating specialisations as oriented edges of D~ minus {omega', omega''}.

In modern terms: positions of D are single-element extensions of the rank-3 oriented matroid defined by Sigma. Stable positions are generic extensions, and specialisation is the weak-map / face order on the extension poset. The page studies the link of a non-generic extension in the extension space, which he expects to be polygonal, i.e. locally 2-manifold-like.
errors: The count of generalisations is self-corrected on the page: 2nu+2nu=4nu in the text, then 'd'ordre 2nu seulement en se bornant aux gén. immédiates' in the footnote. Which nu is meant (number of vertices of Sigma on Delta, or total local multiplicity) is not determinable from the legible text.

Grothendieck himself flags a gap: specialisation triangles with their orientations do not naturally form a polygonal structure when several exist. The first approach (from stable D) is abandoned here rather than resolved.

The previous page records a counterexample (Sigma = St_{4,3}?) to an expected property, so the general polygonal-link claim may need hypotheses, e.g. immediate generalisations only or simple vertices. The page asserts the identification without proof.

ideas.what: Space/graph of positions of an added pseudo-line relative to a pseudo-line arrangement, ordered by specialisation/generalisation
ideas.modern_name: Extension space (poset of single-element extensions) of a rank-3 oriented matroid
ideas.usually_credited_to: Las Vergnas (single-element extensions, 1978); Sturmfels–Ziegler, 'Extension spaces of oriented matroids' (1993); Mnëv–Ziegler
ideas.where_published: Only allusions to pseudo-lines/'géométrie modérée' themes in Esquisse d'un programme (1984); the pseudo-line notes are unpublished

ideas.what: Immediate generalisations of a non-stable position Delta form a polygon (circle) that double-covers the polygon traced by Delta's lift in the sphere X~, with compatible orientations
ideas.modern_name: Link of a non-generic extension in the extension space being a sphere S^1 (local manifold property); lift to the double cover S^2 -> RP^2
ideas.usually_credited_to: Local structure of extension spaces: Sturmfels–Ziegler 1993 (rank 3 extension spaces are homotopy equivalent to S^2); related generalized Baues problem, Billera–Kapranov–Sturmfels 1994

ideas.what: Specialisation triangles/'cuvettes': a stable line specialises by sweeping across a triangular cell with base on D
ideas.modern_name: Triangle flips / mutations of pseudoline arrangements (Ringel's homotopy theorem)

missed.claim: Grothendieck is studying, independently and around 1983-84, the extension space of rank-3 oriented matroids (positions of a new pseudo-line). He works locally, checking that links of non-generic extensions are polygons, i.e. that the complex of positions is a surface. This anticipates the Sturmfels–Ziegler extension-space results (1993) and the generalized Baues problem, framed in his own 'spécialisation/générisation' language borrowed from scheme theory.
missed.quote: s'identifie aux sommets d'un polygone ... d'ordre 2ν+2ν=4ν ... d'ordre 2 de celui défini par Δ
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical credit: an unpublished early treatment of extension spaces of pseudoline arrangements by Grothendieck. The explicit description of links as double covers of the polygon of Delta in S^2 is a concrete local model that could be compared with known results on topology of extension spaces in rank 3.

missed.claim: The problem of a natural polygonal structure on specialisations of a stable position (several specialisation triangles with orientations) is left open on this page. It is not resolved here and is only partly reformulated on the next page.
missed.quote: L'ennui, c'est que les orientations et spécialisations ne forment pas, avec les autres spéc. et gén. immédiates, une structure polygonale naturelle
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This corresponds to understanding the cell structure dual to the extension poset around generic extensions. That question is open in general for non-realizable arrangements and in higher rank.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a genuine and little-known strand of Grothendieck's work: pseudo-line arrangements and the extension-space-like poset of positions with scheme-theoretic specialisation language, predating Sturmfels–Ziegler. The specific local statement on this page (link of a non-stable position is a polygon double-covering Delta's polygon) is close to what is known in the oriented-matroid literature. It is also partly illegible and self-corrected, so it is notable historically but not a surprising new result.
transcription_corrections: Line 1-3: likely 'Quand il y en a un, l'orientation de D est déterminée par [le fait d']être base des triangles de spécialisation pour D'.
Left column: 'Peut-être est-il plus instructif de partir de Δ, et regarder les liens [?] ...' — the struck line reads 'si D est orientée ou pas'.
Grothendieck's term is likely 'générisations' (as on next page) where the machine reads 'généralisations'.
Right column: 'On fera attention que le polygone n'est pas canonique' is a plausible reading of 'On fait attention par la polygone ... canonique'.
'Types est-il' is probably 'Ainsi est-il' or similar; 'Types, les orbites' in the left column is likely 'Ainsi, les orbites/arêtes'.
Right column top: 'correspondant aux deux orbites de X en ce sommet' — 'orbites' may be 'côtés'.
